about: Papers that empirically validate (or fail to validate) constructs, instruments, or behavioral indicators. Rows are added by the maintainers, from their own reading or from submissions made through the form on empirical_evidence.html.

rows.title: Safetywashing: Do AI Safety Benchmarks Actually Measure Safety Progress?
rows.tldr: Scores dozens of language and vision models on safety benchmarks and on a general capabilities score (first principal component of standard capability benchmarks), then reports the Spearman correlation of each safety benchmark with that score and with training compute.
rows.conclusion: About half of the safety benchmarks studied track general capabilities and compute closely, including alignment (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena), ETHICS, TruthfulQA, scalable oversight (GPQA, QuALITY), static adversarial robustness (ANLI, ImageNet-A), and Brier score calibration. These can be moved by scaling alone, which invites 'safetywashing'. Bias benchmarks, dynamic jailbreak attacks, RMS calibration error, sycophancy, and MACHIAVELLI correlate weakly or negatively, and WMDP hazardous knowledge correlates strongly negatively with safety. The authors recommend that new safety benchmarks report their correlation with capabilities.

rows.title: What AI Benchmarks Actually Measure: Adapting Convergent and Discriminant Validity to Interrogate Fifty-Six AI Benchmarks
rows.tldr: Groups 56 capability and safety benchmarks under the concepts they claim to measure (11 concepts) and scores 53 instruction-tuned models from 31 families on them. Tests convergent and discriminant validity with Spearman correlations of model rankings within and across concepts, in a multitrait-multimethod framing, and repeats the test at the item level with 1PL IRT models. A relabeling test checks whether a benchmark fits another concept better than its own.
rows.conclusion: Safety benchmarks that share a concept often give weakly correlated rankings (refusal, safety detection, and bias are frequently near or below zero), so those concepts are operationalized inconsistently. Reasoning and knowledge benchmarks do not separate from each other. Score format predicts benchmark similarity more strongly than the intended concept. Some benchmarks fit another concept better: BBQ accuracy tracks reasoning and DecodingTrust-Fair tracks knowledge more than bias. Refusal and over-refusal are strongly inversely related. The authors ask benchmark developers to document their concepts' scope and boundaries and release item-level data for ongoing validity checks.
